title: SOLID Principles in C++
description: Comprehensive study of S.O.L.I.D. principles in modern C++ with code smells, anti-patterns, and interactive before-vs-after refactoring architectures.

topics.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
topics.description: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change. Separating business logic, persistence, formatting, and validation.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states: 'A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.' Each class should encapsulate a single, focused responsibility.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: When a class handles multiple responsibilities (e.g., calculating taxes, saving to SQL, and printing HTML receipts), modifying one feature risks breaking all unrelated features.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Separate domain business rules from persistence, reporting, and notification mechanisms.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Split 'God classes' into cohesive cooperating entities: Invoice (business data & calculations), InvoiceRepository (database persistence), and InvoicePrinter (formatting).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: SRP Decomposition Flow:

callout.title: SRP Decomposition
callout.text: Before: Order Class [Calculate Total + Save to MySQL + Send SMTP Email + Generate PDF] (4 reasons to change!)\nAfter: Order (Data) + PricingCalculator + OrderRepository + NotificationService + InvoiceFormatter (1 reason each).

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content:
Lines 6-11: Order only holds state.
Lines 14-19: Tax logic can change without touching database code.
Lines 22-27: Database engine can switch to MongoDB without touching HTML templates.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Layered microservice architecture (Controller -> Service -> Repository -> Serializer).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Always design classes around a single cohesive domain responsibility.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not create 10 micro-classes for a trivial 5-line script (avoid premature over-fragmentation).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: High cohesion, easy unit testing, low merge conflicts in team codebases.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Increases the total number of class files.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: SRP in Domain-Driven Design (Entities, Value Objects, Repositories, Domain Services).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Creating a 'Manager' or 'Helper' class that accumulates dozens of unrelated tasks (God Class smell).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is a code smell that indicates a violation of SRP?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: A class that imports both database libraries (e.g., SQL/Redis) and formatting/presentation libraries (e.g., JSON/HTML), or a class with constructor parameters from unrelated domain contexts.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Refactor a flawed UserAccount that validates passwords, connects to MySQL, and sends SMTP emails into 3 SRP-compliant classes.

refactor.title: SRP UserAccount Refactoring
refactor.problemSummary: UserAccount handles credentials, database persistence, and email delivery.
violations: Tightly coupled to MySQL and SMTP
benefits: Database changes do not affect email logic

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: SRP ensures that changes to one subsystem never introduce regressions into unrelated business logic.

topics.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
topics.description: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification. Leveraging polymorphism to add new features without altering tested code.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP) states: 'Software entities (classes, modules, functions) should be open for extension, but closed for modification.'

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Modifying tested production classes to add new features risks introducing regressions and requires re-testing the entire application.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Add new behavior by writing new subclasses or strategy implementations, not by editing existing if-else or switch chains.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Define abstract interfaces. When a new requirement arrives (e.g. Adding Crypto payment to CreditCard and PayPal), create a new class implementing the interface without modifying the payment dispatcher.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: OCP Architecture:

callout.title: OCP in Action
callout.text: Closed: PaymentProcessor::pay(IPaymentStrategy& method)\nOpen: class ApplePay : public IPaymentStrategy (Zero changes to PaymentProcessor!)

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Extensible Discount Calculation Engine obeying OCP:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Line 32: BlackFridayVipDiscount was added as a new class. CheckoutEngine required zero modifications.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Plugin architectures (Chrome extensions, VS Code language servers, audio VST plugins).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use whenever new variants of a business rule (tax rates, discounts, payment types) are expected to grow over time.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not create abstract hierarchies for static constants that will never vary.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Zero risk of regression bugs in existing, tested code.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires up-front abstraction design.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Strategy Pattern OCP, Template Method OCP, Plugin/Registry OCP.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Modifying a base class and breaking all existing derived subclasses.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does OCP relate to the Strategy and Factory design patterns?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: The Strategy pattern provides the polymorphic extension points for OCP, while the Factory pattern isolates the creation of those strategies in a single location, keeping client business logic closed for modification.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Design a NotificationManager that adheres to OCP when adding Discord and Telegram alerts.

practice.title: OCP Notification Manager
practice.problemStatement: Build notification manager that accepts new channels without modifications.
practice.hint: Loop over vector of INotificationChannel shared_ptr.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: OCP allows systems to grow organically by writing new classes rather than hacking existing ones.

topics.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
topics.description: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering system correctness or violating preconditions/postconditions.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states: 'If S is a subtype of T, then objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering any of the desirable properties of the program.'

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Inheritance without LSP leads to runtime crashes where derived classes throw unexpected exceptions or violate base class contracts (e.g. The classic Square-Rectangle dilemma).

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Derived classes must fulfill the base class contract completely. Preconditions cannot be strengthened; postconditions cannot be weakened; invariants must be preserved.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: A Square is mathematically a rectangle, but in object-oriented programming, setting width independently of height is a base invariant of Rectangle. Square breaks this invariant, so Square MUST NOT inherit from Rectangle!

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: The Classic Square-Rectangle LSP Violation:

callout.title: The Square-Rectangle Trap
callout.text: void resize(Rectangle& r) { r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(10); assert(r.getArea() == 50); }\nIf a Square is passed: setHeight(10) also changes width to 10 -> Area becomes 100 -> Assertion FAILS! LSP is violated.

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Refactoring the Square-Rectangle Dilemma to Obey LSP:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content:
Lines 5-9: IShape defines the common denominator.
Lines 12 & 23: Rectangle and Square both implement IShape independently without corrupting each other's setter contracts.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Read-only file descriptors vs Read-Write file streams in OS virtual file systems.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Always test derived class behavior against base class expectations before creating inheritance links.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Never subclass just to reuse code if the subclass violates any base method contract.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Guarantees safe polymorphic substitution without surprise exceptions.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires rethinking intuitive real-world taxonomies that do not hold in software contracts.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Contract Invariants, Precondition rules, Postcondition rules.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Overriding a base method to throw NotSupportedException.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: If a derived class overrides a virtual method and throws std::runtime_error("Not supported"), is LSP violated?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Yes, absolutely. If the base class contract guarantees that the method succeeds or performs an action, throwing an unsupported exception in a derived class breaks caller expectations and violates LSP. The interface should be segregated instead.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Refactor a ReadOnlyFile that throws on write() into segregated IReadable and IWritable interfaces.

refactor.title: File System LSP Refactoring
refactor.problemSummary: ReadOnlyFile inherits File and throws on write(), violating LSP.
violations: Subtype cannot substitute for base File

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contracts established by their base abstractions.

topics.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
topics.description: Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use. Designing fine-grained, cohesive role interfaces.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) states: 'Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.'

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Fat, bloated interfaces force implementers to write empty dummy methods or throw unsupported exceptions, polluting the architecture.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Split 'Fat Interfaces' into small, client-specific role interfaces (e.g. IPrinter, IScanner, IFax instead of one giant IMachine).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Clients depend only on the minimal role interface they require. Concrete classes can implement multiple small interfaces simultaneously via multiple inheritance.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: ISP Decomposition:

callout.title: Fat Interface vs Role Interfaces
callout.text: Fat: IMultiFunctionDevice [print(), scan(), fax(), staple()] (Simple printer forced to implement fax!)\nSegregated: IPrinter [print()] + IScanner [scan()] + IFax [fax()]. SimplePrinter implements ONLY IPrinter!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Production-Grade ISP Role Interface Design:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content:
Lines 4 & 11: Fine-grained role interfaces.
Line 34: executePrintJob(IPrinter&) requires ONLY printing capabilities, accepting both simple and multi-function hardware.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: C++ standard streams (std::istream for reading, std::ostream for writing, std::iostream combining both).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Always break large interfaces into focused role interfaces.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not create single-method interfaces for operations that are intrinsically coupled and always used together.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Eliminates dummy stub implementations and reduces recompilation cascades.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Increases the number of interface class definitions.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Role Interfaces, Header Interface segregation.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Adding new specialized methods to a general-purpose interface instead of creating a new role interface.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does ISP prevent unnecessary recompilation in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: In C++, if a large header IFatInterface.hpp changes, every translation unit that includes that header must be recompiled. By segregating into small headers (IPrinter.hpp, IScanner.hpp), clients including only IPrinter.hpp are immune to changes in IScanner.hpp, preventing compilation cascades.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Segregate a Worker interface with work() and eat() so that RobotWorker is not forced to implement eat().

practice.title: Worker Interface Segregation
practice.problemStatement: Segregate Worker into IWorkable and IFeedable.
practice.hint: HumanWorker implements both; RobotWorker implements only IWorkable.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: ISP keeps interfaces minimal, client-specific, and decoupled.

topics.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
topics.description: High-level modules should not depend upon low-level modules; both should depend upon abstractions. Abstractions should not depend upon details.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content:
The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) states:
1. High-level modules should not depend upon low-level modules. Both should depend upon abstractions.
2. Abstractions should not depend upon details. Details should depend upon abstractions.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Directly binding high-level business rules to low-level hardware or third-party SDKs makes the core business domain brittle, untestable, and impossible to migrate.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Invert the dependency arrow using pure abstract interfaces. High-level policy owns the interface contract; low-level infrastructure implements it.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: High-level PaymentService defines IPaymentGateway. Low-level StripeSDKAdapter implements IPaymentGateway. PaymentService depends only on IPaymentGateway.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Dependency Inversion Diagram:

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Production C++ Dependency Inversion Architecture:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content:
Lines 6-10: IPaymentProcessor decouples high-level policy.
Line 15: CheckoutService holds an interface pointer, allowing Stripe, PayPal, or unit test Mocks to be swapped effortlessly.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Clean Architecture / Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) in fintech and enterprise trading.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Always apply DIP between high-level business domains and low-level I/O, database, and network services.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not invert dependencies for stable standard library data structures (like std::string or std::vector).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Extreme testability, modularity, and freedom to swap infrastructure technologies.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Adds interface indirection.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Constructor Dependency Inversion, Template-based Static Dependency Inversion.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Instantiating concrete classes with new directly inside high-level service constructors.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP), Dependency Injection (DI), and Inversion of Control (IoC)?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content:
Answer:
• DIP: High-level architectural design principle (depend upon abstractions, not details).
• DI: Specific implementation pattern for fulfilling DIP (passing dependencies via constructor/setter).
• IoC: Broader architectural framework principle where the framework controls execution flow (Hollywood Principle: 'Don't call us, we'll call you').

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Apply DIP to decouple a WeatherDashboard from a concrete OpenWeatherMapApi client using an IWeatherDataSource interface.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: DIP creates resilient software architectures where business policy remains independent of volatile infrastructure details.
